Dear Colleague,

Reason for referral: Evaluation of persistent fatigue in the setting of a strong family history of early heart disease.

I am writing about Julia Sullivan, a 69-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism. She reports several months of persistent fatigue and reduced energy.

Please assess her symptoms in light of a strong family history of early heart disease. Her mother developed heart disease in her early 50s, and her brother developed it before age 60.

Most recent echo showed an ejection fraction of 55%.

Thank you for seeing this patient.

Dr. Kevin Harris

ADMISSION DIAGNOSIS:
Julia Sullivan is a 69-year-old woman admitted for an acute urinary stone causing obstruction. The obstruction produced severe flank discomfort and difficulty passing urine, prompting hospital care. Her established medical conditions include hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypothyroidism. The working diagnosis on arrival was an obstructing ureteral stone with acute symptoms. The immediate goals were relief of the obstruction, control of discomfort, and safe planning for return home. The admitting team reviewed her history and coordinated care with the urology service. No calendar dates, named drugs, numerical results, or study findings are included in this summary. The final diagnosis remained an acute obstructing urinary stone, treated during this stay. Her chronic conditions were considered in decisions about supportive care and discharge planning. She was admitted to the hospital for treatment and observation, with instructions to alert staff if her symptoms changed.
Julia Sullivan | MRN-47879 | Discharge summary | Page 2 of 20

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
Ms. Sullivan reported a sudden episode of flank pain that persisted despite attempts to rest at home. The discomfort was associated with urinary difficulty and nausea, and she could not maintain her usual routine. She denied a recent similar episode requiring hospital care. Her symptoms led to evaluation and recognition of an obstructing urinary stone. The course and location of the stone were reviewed with the treating team, with the priority being relief of the blockage. She was admitted because symptoms remained significant and intervention was considered appropriate. She received supportive care while the urology service reviewed the available clinical information. The record does not include a named study, numerical result, or calendar date. On arrival she was able to provide her history and discuss her preferences. She agreed with a plan focused on treating the obstruction, improving comfort, and arranging follow-up after discharge.
